name: William F. Buckley Jr.
role: American conservative writer, National Review founder and Firing Line host
summary: Buckley defended private enterprise and political decentralization and argued against Cold War coexistence with Soviet communism. He defended white political control in the South in the 1950s and later acknowledged that federal action against Jim Crow had been necessary. He also came to favor ending prohibition of most recreational drugs for adults.

abortion-legal.rationale: In the Firing Line debate Buckley argues that the humanity of fetal life warrants legal protection and that exceptional circumstances of conception do not decide the general case.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Buckley calls for government action against unions that have excluded Black workers and proposes tax deductions for employers who hire Black apprentices to improve their access to skilled trades.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Buckley explicitly opposes prosecuting consenting adults for homosexual conduct in the Civil Liberties Review interview.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Buckley confines public relief to people who remain poor and, in the Four Reforms interview, explicitly rejects federal minimum welfare standards for everyone.

decide-locally.rationale: The founding statement argues that remote government is irresponsible and that freedom requires political decentralization.

democracy-best.rationale: In 1957 Buckley defended allowing a white minority to override local election outcomes. In 1970 he continued to argue for restricting the franchise on grounds of political knowledge.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Buckley questions whether a free electoral victory for Milosevic would make his regime acceptable and distinguishes elections in Iraq from a durable democratic reorientation.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: Buckley’s founding statement calls the convergence of the two major parties a serious danger and calls for a two-party system that openly contests political differences.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Buckley argues that greenhouse gas emissions exceed what nature can absorb and urges conservatives to support Kyoto’s binding emissions limits and trading system despite their expected costs.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The founding statement rejects surrendering American sovereignty to a world organization and singles out the United Nations.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Buckley explicitly favors preferential hiring of Black workers in conditions of low unemployment and proposes tax incentives for employers who take on Black apprentices.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In 1957 Buckley defended white control over Black majorities. By 1970 he opposed denying constitutional rights because of race, and in 2004 explicitly said he had been wrong to count on Jim Crow ending without federal intervention.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Defending Four Reforms, Buckley confirmed his proposal for a federal income tax at a flat 15 percent.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Buckley argues that expecting immigrants to learn English was an important means of integrating them and criticizes policies he says have removed that expectation.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Buckley recounts his earlier opposition and explains why he came to favor allowing the sale of most drugs to adults after concluding that prohibition had failed.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Buckley favors licensing brothels because he considers a legal, regulated market better able to address health risks than prohibition.

limit-guns.rationale: Buckley opposes strict curbs on ordinary pistol and rifle ownership for self-defense while rejecting an unlimited individual right to every kind of weapon.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Buckley calls competitive pricing indispensable to material progress and treats expansion of government control as a threat to that system.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Buckley defends the 2003 Iraq intervention and says the United States should be prepared to use force to preserve Taiwan’s independence in the face of a coercive ultimatum from Beijing.

more-religion-public.rationale: Buckley tells PBS that separating Christianity entirely from politics is a serious mistake because he considers religion a principal source of a harmonious political community.

negative-income-tax.rationale: In the Playboy interview Buckley endorses replacing existing welfare measures with the Nixon–Moynihan Family Assistance Plan, an income floor with benefits reduced as family earnings rose.

one-party-rule.rationale: Buckley committed his magazine to a competitive two-party system and described the prospect of a single political tendency controlling both major parties as a danger.

open-borders.rationale: Buckley rejects unrestricted entry as a principle in the immigration debate and argues that the country may limit admissions to preserve its capacity for assimilation.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: Buckley praises worship in underground churches despite a legal ban and argues that subjects of a totalitarian state ought to defy their rulers.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Buckley favors pricing pollution and argues that a graduated charge would curb motorists’ pollution more effectively than a legal limit on engine power.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Buckley explicitly calls preserving the country’s culture and civic ethos a legitimate goal of immigration policy.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Buckley describes the state’s role as asserting a victim’s rights in an adversarial trial and explains how that public responsibility also requires protecting innocent defendants.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Buckley defends the attempt to foster a democratic political order in Iraq and presents promoting peace and liberty overseas as a continuing American aim.

property-fundamental.rationale: In Individualism at Yale, Buckley defends private property as indispensable to personal freedom and criticizes treating it as a convenience the state can set aside.

public-ownership.rationale: In Individualism at Yale, Buckley criticizes the textbook program that treats nationalizing major businesses as a substitute for competition and presents that program as an encroachment on economic freedom.

racial-franchise.rationale: Buckley’s 1957 defense of white control included overriding Black votes. In 1970 he expressly rejected withholding the franchise on racial grounds while still favoring a political knowledge qualification, and later repudiated his earlier stance on federal intervention against Jim Crow.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Buckley defended white political control in 1957 but said in the 1970 interview that he favored equal access to public accommodations. He accepted the antidiscrimination principle of Brown in the Four Reforms discussion and later said federal intervention against Jim Crow had been necessary.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In the Playboy interview Buckley describes minimum wage laws as a barrier to employment and favors repealing many of them to revive apprenticeships.

reduce-immigration.rationale: On Firing Line Buckley argued for curbing overall immigration and defended a pause to give assimilation time to work.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Buckley explains his reversal on drug prohibition by arguing that a conservative should test whether a legal restriction works in practice and examine the harms it causes.

school-vouchers.rationale: Buckley proposes giving parents a publicly funded voucher equal to the cost of educating a child, redeemable at any public or private school they choose.

separated-powers.rationale: In the introduction to Four Reforms, Buckley argues that executive power is already excessive and defends Congress’s ability to overturn or set aside presidential initiatives.

social-market-economy.rationale: Buckley argues that a private economy should continue reducing poverty, while acknowledging that people who remain poor still need public relief. He proposes redirecting federal welfare funds to poorer states and leaving program design to the states.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Buckley defends an individual right to possess a pistol or rifle for self-defense and discusses the practical value of citizens being able to exercise it.

state-harmful.rationale: Buckley assigns government the necessary task of protecting life, liberty and property and treats the protection of victims and innocent defendants as a reason for state courts.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Buckley argues that matters between worshippers and God lie outside the state’s jurisdiction and that a ban on church attendance voids the obligation to obey it.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Buckley tells Civil Liberties Review he supports wiretapping not only suspected collaborators with foreign intelligence agencies but also a group behind an attempted bombing, subject to legal guidelines.

tax-inheritance.rationale: In Individualism at Yale, Buckley criticizes proposals to use estate and inheritance taxes to eliminate hereditary fortunes and defends the incentive to leave a substantial inheritance.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Buckley proposed a single federal income tax rate of 15 percent and rejected higher rates on higher incomes as a means of redistribution.

work-for-welfare.rationale: His mayoral proposal would require welfare recipients able to work to do municipal cleanup, with exemptions for disability and for mothers caring for younger children.
